title: I Am Death, Destroyer of Worlds
story:
Arjuna looked into the mouth of the universe and saw his own family entering it.

Krishna had given him celestial sight, and what it revealed stood before him like a second sky: a form with a thousand faces and a thousand arms, mouths that blazed like the fire at the end of the ages, bearing diadem, mace, and discus, glowing on every side. The whole universe — gods and beasts, heaven and earth — was gathered into that one body. He saw Brahman seated on his lotus seat, the Rishis and the celestial serpents, the Rudras, the Adityas, the Vasus, the Ashwins and the Maruts; he saw hosts of gods entering the form while others, afraid, prayed with joined hands, and the great Rishis and Siddhas praising it with hymns. The space between heaven and earth, and every point of the horizon, was pervaded by that body; the sun and the moon were its eyes, the blazing fire its mouth. The form was hard to look at — a mass of energy glowing on all sides, touching the very skies, many-hued, with blazing, enormous eyes and its mouth wide open. It had no beginning, no middle, no end; it was indestructible, the supreme object of the universe, heating the whole creation with its own radiance. At the sight of it the triple world trembled, and the hosts of great Rishis and Siddhas praised it with cries of hail, while Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Asuras stared, amazed. "Neither end, nor middle, nor beginning of you do I behold," Arjuna said, with his hair standing on end.

And then he saw what was happening at the mouths. "The sons of Dhritarashtra," he said, "together with the hosts of kings, and Bhishma, and Drona, and Karna the son of the charioteer, with the principal warriors of our own side — all of them are quickly entering your terrible mouths, made fierce by your tusks. Some, with their heads crushed, are caught between the interstices of your teeth. As rivers of many currents roll swiftly toward the ocean, so these heroes of the world of men enter your flaming mouths. As moths rush with increasing speed to the blazing fire for their own destruction, so do these men rush to their doom in you. I can no longer command courage or peace of mind. Be gracious, O God of gods, O refuge of the universe."

And from within that blaze a voice answered — the same voice that had driven the chariot, the same voice that had spoken of the immortal soul. "I am Death," it said, "the destroyer of the worlds, fully developed. I am now engaged in slaying the race of men. By me have all these been already slain. Be only my instrument."

The words fell on Arjuna like a second revelation. The war he had dreaded, the killing he had refused, the kinsmen he could not bear to face — all of it had already happened, in the will of the one who stood before him. The warriors he had seen streaming into those mouths were not about to die; they were already gone. What remained was only whether Arjuna would be the willing instrument, or something less.

The vision blazed around him — mouths and tusks and flame, the splendour of a hundred suns — and Arjuna, trembling, bowed his head in the middle of the blaze. He had asked to see the truth, and the truth was this: the battle was not his to begin or to refuse. It was his to serve, or his to watch in helplessness — and the whole difference between those two, the whole war, lay in that single choice. Still the voice waited for his answer.
reflection: The terrible form is the kindest thing Krishna could have shown him: the war Arjuna fears to cause has already happened — the warriors are already gone. His choice is not whether they die but whether he will be the willing instrument or the helpless witness, and the whole of the Gita's call to action rests on that strange, liberating knowledge.
content_note: Contains imagery of warriors being drawn into the cosmic form's flaming mouths; intense but not graphic.
next_story_tease: Then, as suddenly, the cosmic form would fold back into the charioteer's gentle shape.
hero_scene: Within the blazing cosmic form, the warriors of both armies stream like rivers into Krishna's flaming, tusk-fierce mouths, while a small Arjuna stands before the vision with joined hands, his hair standing on end.
